title: GlideOS vs Airtable for internal business apps (2026)
summary: GlideOS vs Airtable: Compare data, permissions and user access, and discover a better way to build your internal business app with AI.
body_markdown:
Your team tracks every job in an Airtable base. Project managers update statuses, finance pulls hours at the end of the month, and the operations lead spends Friday afternoon chasing whoever forgot to tick a box. Then someone forwards Glide’s post about rebuilding Airtable setups in GlideOS, and the question lands on your desk: should we move?


Both tools can run an internal app. They just start from opposite ends. Airtable starts from your data and adds screens on top. GlideOS starts from the app and asks an AI agent to build everything around it. This guide compares the two on what matters once real people use the app every day: how you build it, where the data lives, who can log in, what each person sees, and how the cost grows.


## What is the difference between GlideOS and Airtable?


Airtable is a relational database with a spreadsheet look. Your records sit in bases and tables, and you add Interfaces when you want people to work through screens instead of grids. Most internal Airtable apps start life as a shared base and grow into something the whole team depends on.


GlideOS is an app builder. Glide[announced it in June 2026](https://community.glideapps.com/t/introducing-glideos/87253) as “our new AI builder for internal business apps” and renamed its original visual builder Glide Classic. In GlideOS, you describe what you need, and Glide’s AI agent builds the screens, the data, and the logic. The app is the product; the database sits underneath it.


Why does this matter? Because an internal app is only useful if people can find what they need without asking someone. Teams spend 25% of their time just searching for answers, according to[Atlassian’s State of Teams 2025 report](https://www.atlassian.com/blog/state-of-teams-2025) , a survey of 12,000 knowledge workers and 200 executives. Whichever tool you choose, the test is the same: does each person open the app and see their next job, their own records, and nothing they shouldn’t?

## How do you build an internal app in GlideOS vs Airtable?


**In GlideOS, you build by chatting.** You describe the app, upload a spreadsheet, or pick a data source such as Airtable, and the AI agent creates the first version. To move a button, add a field, or change a rule, you ask the agent again. There’s no drag-and-drop editor, so every layout change goes through the chat. Building uses AI credits, and so do AI features, workflows, and some integrations once the app is live. You can check what each plan includes on[Glide’s pricing page](https://www.glideapps.com/pricing) .


**In Airtable, you build from your tables.** You set up the base first, then use the Interface Designer to arrange records into pages, lists, forms, and dashboards. Since April 2026, Omni, Airtable’s AI assistant, can[generate custom interface elements on every plan](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/airtable_creating-custom-interface-elements-with-omni-activity-7449847743285497856-LKlx) , and generating them doesn’t use AI credits. You still decide where everything goes by hand, which some teams prefer and others find slow.


A simple way to choose: if the person building the app thinks in tables and fields, Airtable will feel natural. If they’d rather describe the outcome (“a page where each project manager sees their own open jobs and can mark them done”), GlideOS will feel faster at the start.


## Where does your data live in each tool?


In Airtable, the data stays in your base. Every Interface, automation, and report reads from the same tables, so there’s one copy of the truth.


In GlideOS, you can start a project from an Airtable base by connecting it with an API key. But Glide’s own guide to[switching from Airtable to GlideOS](https://www.glideapps.com/blog/glideos-airtable-alternative) describes importing your bases, tables, records, and relationships so that “your database lives in Glide.” Before you build, ask whether changes made in the app will write back to Airtable, or whether you’re moving the data for good. If finance, reporting, or other tools still read from the Airtable base, a one-way copy will leave those tools working from old numbers.


## Who can log in, and what can each person see?


This is where internal apps usually get complicated. A 40-person firm doesn’t have one kind of user. Project managers need to edit their jobs, technicians need their schedule on a phone, finance needs hours and rates, and only directors should see margins.


**GlideOS** lets you invite unlimited guests to published apps, while builders count as paid team members. Glide says roles and rules that limit each user to their own rows are part of the product. On the pricing page, the Free plan can’t publish apps, the Basic plan publishes apps for your team, public apps start on Plus, org-level roles and permissions come with Pro, and project-level roles with Enterprise. Check which plan covers the roles you need before you build.


**Airtable** charges per editor: anyone who changes records needs a paid seat, while read-only viewers are free. In Interfaces, you can filter which records a person sees on a page, but per-field control is limited, so hiding a single column such as “margin” from one group often means building a separate page. People outside your company need the Portals add-on, which is priced per guest; see[Airtable’s pricing page](https://airtable.com/pricing) . We compare these limits in more detail in[Noloco vs Airtable Interfaces](https://noloco.io/noloco-vs-airtable-interfaces) .


On phones, GlideOS has the edge out of the box: Glide builds every app to work on a small screen first. Airtable has mobile apps and Interfaces open on phones, but you design layouts on a desktop, so test them on a phone before you hand them to field staff.


## What changed at Airtable in 2026, and does it matter for your decision?


Bending Spoons completed its purchase of Airtable in September 2026. In October, Airtable said that “for customers, nothing changes regarding your plan, price, or service offering” in[its post on what’s next](https://www.airtable.com/newsroom/back-to-bases) . The same post confirmed that a large share of Airtable’s previous team is leaving, and laid out plans for an upgraded Omni, Airtable Canvas for building custom apps, and better external collaboration.


For most teams, this isn’t a reason to rebuild tomorrow. It is a reason to keep your options open: avoid locking your data into any single tool’s format, and know how you’d move if prices or priorities change. We cover the deal in more detail in[what the Bending Spoons acquisition means for Airtable users](https://noloco.io/blog/bending-spoons-airtable-acquisition-whats-next) .


GlideOS has its own version of this question. It’s a separate product from Glide Classic, with its own subscription and no way to bring Classic apps across. If your team already has apps in Glide Classic, read[why moving from Glide Classic to GlideOS is a rebuild](https://noloco.io/blog/migrate-from-glide-classic-to-glideos-a-rebuild) before you plan anything.


## Where does Noloco fit for internal business apps?


Noloco is an AI portal builder for businesses whose operations don’t fit a template, and that includes apps used only by your own team. It sits between the two approaches above: you keep your data where it is, like Airtable, and you can build by describing the app to AI, like GlideOS. You can also open the visual builder and change things yourself.


Here’s what that looks like for an internal app:


- **Keep your Airtable base.**[Connect your existing base](https://noloco.io/data/airtable) and edits sync both ways, so nothing moves and reports that read from Airtable keep working. You can also combine Airtable with Google Sheets, Postgres, MySQL, or Noloco’s own database in the same app.
- **Build with AI or by hand.** Describe the app to[Nola, Noloco’s AI builder](https://noloco.io/product/nola) : “Build a jobs app where each project manager sees only their own projects, technicians see their schedule for the week, and finance sees hours and rates.” Then fix a label or move a field in the visual builder without spending a prompt.
- **Control what each role sees.** Set[permissions](https://noloco.io/product/permissions) by role down to the table, page, record, and field. Technicians see their jobs but never the rates. Directors see margins; nobody else does.
- **Automate the follow-up.** Use[workflows](https://noloco.io/product/workflows) to send reminders, request sign-offs, and update statuses, so the operations lead stops chasing people on Fridays.
- **Grow without re-pricing every login.** The Free plan includes unlimited team seats and 50 active clients. The Build plan includes 10 team seats (then $5 for each extra seat) and 1,000 active clients. If the app later needs to let clients, subcontractors, or partners in, it’s the same app on the same plan.[See Noloco pricing](https://noloco.io/pricing) .


Enpal, a solar company, uses Noloco this way for its own field sales team. Sales reps, team leaders, and regional managers each log in and see only their own customers, team, or region.[Read the Enpal story](https://noloco.io/customer-stories/enpal) . For a direct side-by-side with Glide’s new builder, see[Noloco vs GlideOS](https://noloco.io/compare/noloco-vs-glideos) .


## Which one should you choose for your internal app?


Start with how your team works today, not with the feature list. These are the situations where each tool tends to fit best:


- **Choose Airtable** if your work already lives in a well-organized base, most users are staff who edit records at a desk, and simple record filters are enough to control who sees what.
- **Choose GlideOS** if you’re starting fresh, your users are mostly on phones, you’re comfortable moving your data into Glide, and you’re happy to make every change by chatting with an AI agent.
- **Choose Noloco** if you want to keep your Airtable base, need different roles to see different fields, want to build with AI and still edit by hand, or expect the app to involve more people over time.

## Final thoughts


GlideOS and Airtable both build internal apps, but they ask different things of you. Airtable asks you to think in tables and charges for every person who edits. GlideOS asks you to move your data into Glide and build everything through chat.


Before you pick, write down three things: who logs in, what each person should and shouldn’t see, and which other tools read from your data. That list usually makes the choice for you.
